videos.title: 1.0 TCE engine problems in Renault and Dacia vehicles
videos.transcript_text:
The 1.0 TCE engine is the 3-cylinder turbocharged 
petrol unit used in Renault and Dacia vehicles.
It was first introduced in 2018 as the TCE 100 
H4Dt engine in the Clio and Capture. It was also
downgraded to TCE 90 later to fit into ecology 
rules. Then it was updated to the TCE 110 H5Dt
in 2020 and used in the Megane. Also, this engine 
was largely used in all Dacia models. And the same
engine was used in the Nissan Micra as the HR10DET 
with a different plastic cover and a Nissan logo,
but all technologies were the same.
When it comes to common problems,
I wouldn’t say these engines were as bad as they 
were originally expected to be. One of the common
issues is significant random punching in early 
model years between 2018 and 2020. But there was
a software update that fixed this issue. So if you 
experience a sudden loss of power, contact your
Renault dealership and have the update installed.
Also, these engines are prone to oil leaks,
especially there is a common leak in 
the valve cover seal. But fortunately,
it’s fixed with the new seal, and it’s a very 
cheap solution, so it's not a big problem here.
These engines use timing chains, and they are 
not eternal. Renault claims that the chain will
last the entire life of the engine, and they 
are not wrong, since when the chain fails,
the engine will die. But, on average, owners hear 
some minor rattling starting at 120,000 miles,
so it makes sense to replace the chain kit 
in these engines at 100,000 miles or 160,000
kilometers to avoid chain jumping or braking. 
It’s quite unpleasant that the phaser may also
require replacement at about 120,000 miles. So, 
if you consider driving your car for a long time,
you should replace the chain kit along with 
the phaser. Also, it’s important to use OEM
oil or at least choose something with 
the needed viscosity to avoid premature
failure of the phaser and chain tensioner. The 
difference between the 100 and 110-horsepower
engines is that the more powerful one has 
two phasers, while the 100-horsepower model
and 90-horsepower model has only an intake 
phaser, which makes it cheaper to service.
Also, the 100-horsepower model has no hydraulic 
lifters, while the more powerful version is
equipped with them. So, if you own the H4Dt model, 
you may need to adjust the valve clearance once
every 60-80 thousand miles. But the procedure 
is only needed when the engine runs roughly and
vibrates or loses power. If it works flawlessly, 
there is no need to invest in valve adjustment.
Also, one more significant difference between the 
two versions of the 1.0 TCE is the fuel injection
system. The 100-horsepower version has port 
injectors that are reliable and don’t usually
cause problems. The 110-horsepower engine has 
direct injection and suffers from intake valve
contamination. This is not a serious problem, but 
just a feature of all direct injection engines
that are used in city traffic and rarely 
run at high revolutions. Sooner or later,
the intake valves will get clogged, and this 
will affect the power and stability of the
engine's work. Fortunately, valve cleaning in 
a good garage is not an expensive service now.
Other than that, I don’t see a lot of problems 
with these engines. For their size and price,
they are quite good machines that have extremely 
low fuel consumption and are good for city driving
with good torque. You will feel a lack of power 
when trying to overtake someone on a highway,
but other than that, the engine 
doesn’t feel extremely underpowered.
Turbochargers sometimes have problems with 
wastegates getting stuck, and you feel a
loss of power and rough running, as well as 
get warnings and lights on the dashboard.
Fortunately, the engine has quite a simple 
turbocharger that is cheap and easy to repair.
I’ve seen some reports for excessive oil 
consumption, but I’m not sure if it’s very
common for these engines. They will certainly 
burn some oil, but as long as it’s less than
half a liter per 1000 miles, it should 
be fine and won’t cause any problems.
So, I don’t think the 1.0 TCE is a bad choice. The 
110-horsepower version seems to be a little more
modern in terms of technologies, but it also 
fails earlier since it powers larger vehicles
like the Megane, and gets a lot of wear and 
tear because of this. The TCE 90 and TCE 100
seem to be solid engines with affordable 
service costs, very good fuel economy,
and they don’t feel extremely underpowered. But, 
of course, like any modern engine, they need
extremely good maintenance to last long enough. 
And I believe 250,000 kilometers or 170,000 miles
is a good average lifespan that you should keep 
in mind if you own a car with such an engine.

videos.title: 0.9 TCE REVIEW, PROBLEMS, RELIABILITY, FAILURES, FUEL CONSUM, TIMING, OIL?
videos.transcript_text:
Welcome to the Autorooto Freak channel.
Greetings to all viewers, subscribers,
supporters. So to the point, the Renault
0.9 TCE engine with its internal code
H4BT or often just H4B is a small 0.9 L
898 CIC cm 3-cylinder turbocharged
gasoline engine. It was introduced by
Renault around 2012 in the Cleo4 and
quickly became a popular choice for
smaller cars in the Renault Nissan
Alliance, including models like the DEA
Sandere, Logan Duster, early versions,
Renault Captor, and even the Smart 44
and Twingo where it's rear mounted. Its
primary goal was to offer good fuel
efficiency and lower emissions through
downsizing. While the turbocharger
compensated for the small displacement
by providing decent power for city and
suburban driving. Review and opinions.
Opinions on the 0.9 tce are somewhat
mixed, reflecting its downsized nature.
For urban driving, it's generally seen
as adequate. The turbo helps with
low-end torque, making it feel
reasonably spritly in traffic and at
lower speeds. On the open road/highway,
its limitations become more apparent. It
can feel strained at higher speeds and
overtaking maneuvers require careful
planning due to its modest power output.
Refinement. Being a threecylinder, it
has a characteristic thrum, especially
at idle and under acceleration. While
some find it charming, others might find
it less refined than four-cylinder
engines. Turbo lag is also a common
complaint, meaning there's a delay
before the power kicks in. Advantages:
Fuel efficiency claimed official figures
often show impressive fuel economy and
low CO2 emissions, contributing to lower
road tax in some regions. Compact and
lightweight, its small size and
lightweight benefit overall vehicle
dynamics and packaging. Good low-end
torque. The turbocharger provides a
useful boost of torque from low RPMs,
which is beneficial in city driving.
Indirect injection. Unlike many modern
turbocharged engines, the 0.9 tce uses
multi-point indirect fuel injection.
This is often cited as a major advantage
for long-term reliability as it avoids
carbon buildup on intake valves, a
common issue with direct injection
engines. Timing chain uses a timing
chain which is generally
maintenance-free for the life of the
engine unlike timing belts that require
periodic replacement. Disadvantages
limited power at higher speeds. The
small displacement means it can struggle
to maintain speed on inclines or during
rapid acceleration at highway speeds.
Noticeable threecylinder
thrum/vibrations.
While balanced, it still has the
inherent characteristic vibrations of a
three-cylinder engine. Turbo lag. There
could be a noticeable delay between
pressing the accelerator and the turbo
spooling up, leading to a slight
hesitation. Less refined for
enthusiastic driving. It's not an engine
for those seeking a sporty driving
experience. Potential for high realworld
fuel consumption. While official figures
are low, aggressive driving or frequent
highway use can significantly increase
actual fuel consumption as the turbo is
constantly working harder. Common faults
and breakdowns. The 0.9 tce is generally
considered more reliable than the
problematic 1.2TC
H5. It overlaps with largely due to its
indirect injection system. However, it's
not without its issues. Thermostat
housing leaks. This is one of the more
frequently reported issues. The plastic
thermostat housing can become brittle
and crack leading to coolant leaks. Oil
and intake manifold/PCV
valve issues. Some owners have reported
oil residue in the intake manifold which
can sometimes be linked to a stuck or
faulty crankase ventilation PCV valve.
While not as severe as the oil burning
in the 1.2TCE,
it's worth monitoring. Low compression
on cylinders. Rare but severe. There are
isolated but concerning reports of low
compression in individual cylinders,
especially cylinder 2, often at
relatively low mileage, eg 36k m. This
can be a sign of internal engine damage
requiring significant repair or engine
replacement. The exact cause isn't
always clear without stripping the
engine, but it highlights a potential
serious mechanical vulnerability.
Ignition coil/spark plug issues. Like
many modern engines, faults with
ignition coils or spark plugs can lead
to misfires and rough running.
Turbocharger issues. While generally
durable for a small turbo, isolated
failures can occur. As with any forced
induction engine, these often present as
a loss of power or unusual noises. Fuel
consumption. Official combined fuel
consumption figures for the 0.9 TCE90HP
often range from 4.3 to 4.7L/100KM.
Real world consumption varies widely
based on driving style and conditions.
Owners on forums report figures from 5.0
to 6.5 L/100km
for mixed driving with careful drivers
sometimes achieving lower. It can reach
7.0 0 to 8.0 L/100 km in heavy city
traffic or with very aggressive driving
on a highway as the small engine has to
work harder. Timing. The Renault 0.9 tce
H4BT engine uses a timing chain. This is
a positive point for long-term ownership
as timing chains are designed to last
the life of the engine and do not
require regular replacement like timing
belts. However, issues with chain
stretch or tensioners can still occur,
though less frequently than in some
other engines. Autodoc even suggests a
recommended part replacement interval of
every 150,000 km for the timing chain,
implying it's not strictly for life in
all cases. Oil oil type. Renault
typically specifies engine oils
conforming to Renault RN07000
or Renault RN0710
standards for the 0.9 tce. Common
viscosities include 5W, 30 or 5W 40,
adhering to ACIA A3/B4
or ACIA C3 specifications. Always check
your vehicle's owner's manual for the
precise recommended oil type and
specification for your specific model
and year. Oil capacity. The oil capacity
for the 0.9 tce H4BT is typically around
4.2 to 4.3 L. Importance. Using the
correct specification and highquality
oil is crucial for the longevity of this
small turbocharged engine, especially
for the turbocharger and timing chain.
Given the engine's compact nature,
regular oil changes at recommended
intervals or even slightly more
frequently for heavy urban use are
highly advisable. Versions and history.
Initial release. The 0.9 tce
debuted around 2012, notably in the
Renault Cleo 4. Power output. Most
common version is the TC90 90HP/66
kW. There was also a TCE75,
75HP/56KW
and a higher output TCE 110, 109HP/80KW
found in sportier versions like the
Twingo GT. application found in a wide
range of compact cars and small SUVs
across the Renault Nissan Mitsubishi
Alliance including Renault Cleo 4,
Captor Eye, Twingo 3, Dea Sander 2,
Logan 2, Docker, Logi, Early Duster Eye,
Smart for 4, Smart42 as part of the
Daimler collaboration. It has largely
been superseded by the newer 1.0TCE, 0
tce, H4DT/H5DT,
and 1.3TC,
H5H engines in more recent models. In
summary, the Renault 0.9TCE
H4BT engine is a good choice for urban
and suburban driving, offering decent
efficiency and enough power for its
intended purpose. Its indirect injection
system is a notable reliability
advantage over some direct injection
counterparts. However, its small size
means it can feel strained on highways
and potential buyers should be aware of
known issues like thermostat housing
leaks and rare but serious low
compression problems. Regular and
diligent maintenance, especially with
the correct engine oil, is key to its
long-term reliability. Thank you for
watching the video and I invite you to
subscribe to the Autorooak channel.
Greetings to everyone and see you in the
next episode. See you soon.

if you performed a compression test on a
cylinder and the results are out of
specs the next step is to perform a leak
down test also known as a cylinder leak
test it measures the percentage of air
escaping from the combustion chamber
when performing the leak down test the
engine should be at operating
temperature the tools required to
complete this test are the engine leak
down test kit and a mechanic's
stethoscope
[Music]
the procedure is as follows start by
removing all spark plugs using a dial
indicator or the timing marks set the
piston to the top dead center of the
compression stroke or TDC on the
cylinder you want to check it's
important to remember that some engines
may need to be locked in position before
performing the test here's a tip if
checking more than one cylinder follow
the engines firing order it will save
time refer to the shop manual for engine
specifications connect the leak down
tester to an adequate air supply and set
the gauge needle to zero install a gauge
adapter into the spark plug hole to
supply the combustion chamber with air
pressure keep in mind that all testers
have specific instructions on gauge
operation and required pressure refer to
the gauge manufacturer's instructions
for details be careful if the engine is
not locked it could turn over when air
pressure is applied to the cylinder
remove any crankshaft turning tools and
keep hands clear prior to connecting the
air source note the amount or the
percentage of leakage to compare with
the specifications in the shop manual in
general a zero to fifteen percent
leakage means the engine condition is
excellent between sixteen to twenty five
percent is good between twenty six to
forty percent is fair but with reduced
performance and forty one percent and
higher means the engine is in poor
condition and needs to be diagnosed and
repaired once the test is completed if
your results are out of specs it could
mean that the piston was not set on top
dead center of the cam
stroke but a TDC of the exhaust stroke
which would have caused the valves to be
open during valve overlap you need to
rotate the crankshaft one full turn and
then perform the test once again if the
results are still out of specs a
diagnosis is required a high leak down
measurement in a cylinder indicates air
is escaping you need to find out exactly
where air is escaping from start the
diagnosis at the easiest and most
accessible points air bubbles coming out
of the coolant tank indicate that air is
escaping to the coolant system most
probably through the cylinder head
gasket this can be confirmed by using a
chemical block tester other
possibilities of such issues are a
cracked cylinder head or engine block or
the cylinder head screws are loose to
check the following points you may need
to listen for air leaks using a mechanic
stethoscope for example you can remove
an exhaust sensor the oil dipstick or
any other easy to remove component air
escaping from the intake port or the
throttle body means one or more intake
valves is leaking air escaping from the
exhaust port means leaking exhaust
valves if air is escaping into the
crankcase area then you may have an
excessively worn cylinder worn or broken
piston rings or a damaged piston
here are a few hints and tips to help
you confirm your diagnosis white exhaust
smoke out of the tailpipe can indicate a
leak to the cooling system if the
combustion pressure leaks to the cooling
system the increased pressure will cause
the coolant system cap to open and let
pressure vent carbon deposits a burg
valve face damaged valve seat or bent
valve stem can cause the valves to leak
blue exhaust smoke out of the tailpipe
can indicate damaged or worn piston ring
Zoara valve stem seals however when the
valve seals of the cause the smoke will
be noticeable mostly upon engine startup
as the oil seeps past the seals when the
engine is stopped if you suspect an
excessive leak to the crankcase add a
teaspoon of engine oil through the spark
plug hole and perform the leak down test
once again the oil will help temporarily
seal the Rings and confirm your
diagnosis thanks for watching
